comment_text: Obviously Brian Cox is a much smarter man than I am when it comes to quantum mechanics, but I'm a 58 yr old guy who has poked around this landscape for my whole life.  And I think he really missed a few major points to make the picture complete.  His explanation focused exclusively on how you can see/visit/understand the quantum world of particles by understanding that (1) you need to know the distances we're talking about and (2) the idea that you can only know a particle's location probabilistically.  But what about other, key ideas such as the double slit experiment that introduces the idea that quantum particles can be both a wave or a particle until they are observed, upon which they collapse into their state of being.  He should mention this phenomena in conjunction with the concept of Schrödinger's cat, probably the most important metaphor in quantum mechanics.  He should also mention the Pauli exclusion principle that describes more about the actions / interactions of particles.  He should also talk about Heisenberg's principle that says you can know two things about a particle - its velocity and its location - but you can only know each of them with decreasing accuracy as your knowledge of the other's accuracy improves.  Its the most basic trade-off in all of quantum mechanics.  These ideas, which he could have explained in another 45 seconds, would give you a fuller picture of how particles move about at the quantum level.

I am retired and thought I might teach myself quantum mechanics. To my surprise, the maths wasn't going to be the hard part, as I was a maths major and had even covered Hilbert spaces (without applications 😂) before. 

Since I also understood abstract algebra, which doesn't need a physical underpinning to define structure, actions and observe results, then even the so called wierdness of quantum mechanics was no more wierd than manipulating objects by rules defined by pure thought. 

The hardest thing I fined in quantum mechanics is the interpetations given for what happens in real experiments involving light and small particles such as electrons. The reasons given for why the results are the way they are often differ for author to author, or more correctly, from what level of sophistication you are getting your understanding from. The confused explainations around the double slit experient involving "particles 😂" are hilariously. It is sometime like being told a bedtime story that you are just expected to accept 😂.

Still, it is the struggle that is interesting rather than only the destination. I started reading Susskind's book on the theoretical minimum on quantum mechanics and stopped halfway through to read and finish his book on the theoretical minimum in classical mechanics before continuing further on his quantum mechanics book. His intuition is great and cuts right to the important ideas, although the mathematical rigour is less (on purpose) than I'd like. Even this is good for me, as it forces me to another source to look at the rigour behind his ideas. 

I am halfway through Susskinds books on special and general relativity too. These are great at cutting directly to the essential without cluttering everything up with rigour, which I now do for myself 😂. 

I am beginning to think that we humans will never understand the true nature of reality, but that quantum mechanics is useful for calculating results about what we perceive to be reality 😂.

I have almost come to the conclusion that  spacetime and particles etc are emergent phenomena caused by some vast quantum object driving every action in the universe (not God 😂). 

With this model in my head I find it easy to imagine that between observations, an election isn't "everywhere" and in fact is "nowhere" and it just "emerges" when acted on in accordance with the rules of quantum mechanics. 

It amazes me that we have even uncovered the rules of quantum mechanics, even slthough they were forced upon us by observation. 

I suspect quantum mechanics might be vastly more complicated than we can image and he might discover more of it, or at least at a deeper level with experiments we as yet can't even image designing.

I’ve been thinking about the measurement problem and superposition, and I believe the standard language (“collapse of the wave function upon observation”) is unnecessarily mystical. Here is a simpler, more intuitive model:

Imagine I am a particle in a lab with 10 scientists. I have a device that freezes their time completely. While they are frozen, I can go left, right, up, down, through every possible path in the lab simultaneously — because time doesn’t constrain me. From their perspective (if they could somehow perceive it), I would appear to be doing everything at once.
When they “measure” me by restarting their time, they don’t collapse my wave function through observation. They simply catch me in one single position at that moment — whichever state I happened to be in when their time resumed. They see a particle, not the full wave.
This removes the spooky “consciousness collapses reality” element. The transition is simply the boundary between a timeless quantum domain and our timed classical world.
I believe this model explains the double-slit experiment cleanly without mysticism and aligns with ideas like emergent time in quantum gravity.

comment_text: The idea of light sometimes behaving like a particle and sometimes like a wave is, at best, a misleading oversimplification.  I can't really blame Crash Course in particular, as it's a very common explanation, but it's wrong.  Light is _always_ a wave _and_ it's _always_ a particle.  The thing to realize is that it's _never_ a _classical_ particle.  In quantum mechanics, the word "particle" has a very specific meaning -- it's just shorthand for "localized wave function."  Essentially, a quantum particle is just a tiny wave.  A _very_ tiny wave, which is why it often acts like what we think of classical particles.  But it's never actually a classical particle.  It's _always_ a wave.  What the photo-electric effect proved is that light was quantized -- that means it's a particle in the quantum mechanics sense of the word, but honestly, sometimes it's just easier to forget about particles altogether, because the word has such a strong connotation of "tiny solid sphere", at least for me.

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle makes intuitive sense to me. When something moves a lot, you're less certain about where it is at any point in time--it could accelerate, friction might apply, the thing might slow. For super small particles, like on the quantum level, this uncertainty is so pronounced that you can't _ever_ know position and momentum.
